prompt: Write the checks that catch a sorter which secretly modifies the caller's array, one that only works on already-sorted input, and one that dies on a single element. Complete isCorrect in the starter file, then run the tests.
explanation: A method can return exactly the right answer and still be broken, because correctness includes what it does to the rest of the world: the in-place sorter hands back a perfectly sorted array while quietly rewriting the caller's data, and the only way to see it is to keep a record of the input and re-inspect it after the call. An already-sorted fixture is worse than useless for a sort -- it is passed by implementations that barely sort at all -- so the input has to be genuinely out of order. The one-element array is the boundary case where a special-case shortcut turns into an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException.
hints: Sort something genuinely jumbled, such as {5, 3, 1, 4}. An input that is already in order is passed even by an implementation that makes a single pass.
After each call, look at the array you passed IN: java.util.Arrays.equals(jumbled, new int[] {5, 3, 1, 4}) must still be true, or the implementation had a side effect.
Add the small boundary inputs -- an empty array, a one-element array, and an array with duplicates -- and wrap everything in try/catch that returns false.
